card.band: 8 h. Several independent levers (CSR, heap, bidirectional, CH, parallel), so partial credit rises steadily. Frontier agents get bidirectional and CSR and some reach CH; a weaker model stops at a minor constant-factor gain. Data has known errors, noted.
card.cheat: Caching answers is closed because queries are hidden and the graphs differ from the visible one. Distances must match exactly and the preprocessing time counts.
card.grading: Hard gate: exact distances against a Dijkstra reference on hidden random query pairs and on hidden larger graphs. Wall-clock medians of total preprocess plus query batch. Reward 2^u-1 against our reference speedup.
card.reference: Our own contraction hierarchies implementation with a measured speedup on the hidden graphs; speedup is measured at grading, not quoted.
card.source: https://www.diag.uniroma1.it/challenge9/download.shtml, public-domain data (USA road graphs; PTV Europe excluded)
card.task: /app ships a plain Dijkstra baseline in C++ or Rust, a loader for the .gr format, and a mid-size graph (such as NY/BAY, about 0.3M nodes) for local checks. The agent makes point-to-point queries and a one-to-all mode faster using layout, heaps, bidirectional search, preprocessing (contraction hierarchies, ALT) and parallelism.
card.title: Road network shortest-path query and preprocessing speedup on DIMACS graphs

source_notes: q:"the files available at this page contain data/software in the public domain". Page also warns q:"the data has numerous errors, in particular gaps in major highways and bridges." Good for multi-lever graph work (CSR layout, heap, bidirectional, preprocessing, parallel). Overlap: none with excluded list (networkx VF2 is different). Travel-time variant files of similar size.
source_version: n/a (input set); pairing = plain Dijkstra baseline vs later CH/delta-stepping code

facts.claim: DIMACS 9th challenge download page lists USA road graphs with distance and travel-time .gr files, including NY (264,346 nodes, 733,846 arcs) and BAY (321,270 nodes, 800,172 arcs)
Page states the files are in the public domain ('the files available at this page contain data/software in the public domain'); no specific licence named
Page warns the data has numerous errors, in particular gaps in major highways and bridges
.gr format: problem line 'p sp n m' first, arc lines 'a U V W' with signed integer weights, node IDs 1..n, c comment lines; .co coordinate files 'p aux sp co n' and 'v id X Y'
Customizable CH paper reports NY (264k vertices) plain Dijkstra about 16,303 us per query versus about 34 us for CH queries (search-snippet level, not fetched in full)
A published CH timing for the DIMACS BAY graph
RoutingKit (public C++ CCH library, KIT) is BSD-2-Clause licensed
Our own CH reference implementation exists and has a measured speedup on the hidden graphs
Frontier agents reach bidirectional, CSR and some CH on this kind of task (dated public evidence)
Hidden larger graphs and query sets are sealed from the agent's image

full_card.band: 8 h tier. Frontier agents plausibly reach CSR, heap, bidirectional and some CH inside 8 h. Weaker model likely stops at constant-factor gains. Convex 2^u-1 reward means low-speedup buckets earn little, so 'steady' credit is doubtful. No dated agent evidence found.
full_card.build_cost: About 3-5 days: write the baseline, loader, CH reference and harness, then calibrate speedup. Smoke build skipped (no git source), so nothing is pre-verified.
full_card.deliverable: Faster point-to-point query path plus one-to-all mode, plus any preprocessing (CSR layout, heap, bidirectional, CH/ALT, threads). Output must give exact distances.
full_card.gates_anticheat: Exact distances vs Dijkstra gate (hard, scores 0). Preprocessing time counted, so per-query caching cannot pay off on hidden queries. Hidden graphs differ from the visible one, so tuning to the sample graph does not transfer. Still to specify: block reading of hidden data and editing of the grader or build config.
full_card.grading_surface: Hidden random s-t pairs and one-to-all runs on hidden USA-derived graphs; exact-match hard gate; wall-clock medians of preprocessing plus query batch. Count of hidden graphs and queries not yet fixed.
full_card.local_fit: Fits 8 cores and 16 GB for NY/BAY-size work. Full-USA-size hidden graphs (up to 24M nodes) may stress memory under CH preprocessing; hidden graph sizes must be capped.
full_card.lookup: CH and CCH are published and well known; public implementations exist (RoutingKit, OSRM) but none is installable offline. A model could recall the algorithm in outline, not the reference code. Verdict partial.
full_card.provenance: DIMACS 9th Implementation Challenge USA road networks (public domain per page); NY and BAY are real DIMACS instances; PTV Europe excluded. Real paper trail: Dibbelt/Strasser/Wagner CCH (arXiv 1402.0402) reports NY timings.
full_card.reference: Our own CH implementation, not yet written; speedup measured at grading. No public permissive reference shipped. Public CH code exists elsewhere (RoutingKit, OSRM) but is not in the image.
full_card.ships: Plain Dijkstra C++ or Rust baseline, .gr/.co loader, NY or BAY graph for local checks, history-less snapshot. Hidden larger USA graphs and query sets are not shipped.
full_card.similarity: Nearest neighbours: S-op-011 0.222, shortest_path_dijkstra (AlgoTune) 0.201, S-im-038 0.156, S-op-014 0.145. Above 0.15 and same subject as AlgoTune Dijkstra, but a different deliverable. Not on the CROWDED list.

Band.why: Frontier agents plausibly reach CH inside 8 h, but there is no dated public agent evidence, so the score is capped at 3.

Build.why: Roughly 3-5 days to write the baseline, loader, CH reference and harness.

Fit.why: CPU-only and within 8 cores / 16 GB for NY/BAY; the largest hidden graphs need a size cap.

Hor.why: Several levers in sequence (layout, heap, bidirectional, CH, threads) suit an 8 h tier.

Lic.why: Public-domain data statement confirmed, though no specific licence is named; our own code is shippable.

Multi.why: Levers are independent, but the convex 2^u-1 reward makes early credit small, so partial credit is less steady than claimed.

Nov.why: Neighbours above 0.15 exist (0.222, 0.201, 0.156); the AlgoTune Dijkstra task shares the subject but not the deliverable.

Real.why: Official DIMACS challenge data with the page and format spec confirmed; NY/BAY sizes match.

Ref.why: Our own CH reference is not built yet, so the measured speedup is unknown; upstream CH timings are published for NY only.

Seal.why: Hidden graphs are public DIMACS files but the agent has no network at run time; CH code is public but not in the image, and recall is a Band question.

Surf.why: Hidden random pairs, one-to-all runs and larger graphs give a deep surface; the count of hidden graphs is not fixed yet.

spike_plan.kill_if: CH over bidirectional is under 10x on BAY, or distances mismatch, or timing noise exceeds 10% across repeats.
spike_plan.pass_if: CH matches Dijkstra on all sampled pairs; CH over bidirectional gives at least 10x median per-query speedup on BAY; run-to-run noise under 10%.
steps: In a throwaway networked container, download NY.gr.gz, NY.co.gz and the BAY distance files from the DIMACS page; confirm they parse with the .gr format (p sp n m).
Write a plain Dijkstra baseline and a bidirectional Dijkstra in C++; check both agree on 1000 random pairs.
Write a minimal CH (node ordering by edge difference, witness search, bidirectional upward query); check exact distance match with Dijkstra on 1000 pairs.
Time median per-query and per-batch (preprocessing included) for Dijkstra, bidirectional and CH on NY and BAY at batch sizes 100, 10k, 1M; record the speedup ratios.
Repeat each timing 5 times to measure noise; then rerun the CH batch inside a gVisor-like setting if available, or note the gap.
Check that the speedup is determined by the algorithm, not the machine: compare CH vs bidirectional ratio across two runs.

v1.summary: The DIMACS source, public-domain data statement, data-error warning, .gr format and NY/BAY sizes are confirmed, and no near-duplicate kill applies (top neighbour 0.222, not crowded). Main risks are that the reference is unbuilt, the convex 2^u-1 reward makes partial credit less steady than claimed, and Band has no dated agent evidence (E0), so the 8 h tier and 3-5 day build need the spike before acceptance.

v2.note: Real public-domain DIMACS data, and the .gr format is confirmed. The equivalence gate is sound. Risk: contraction hierarchies are one dominant, well-known lever. A frontier agent that writes a solid CH may match our reference (K8), and one that does not gets little under the convex 2^u-1 reward, so credit is not steady. Set the reference ceiling above textbook CH (tuned ordering, PHAST for one-to-all, parallel preprocessing) so a band exists. Fix the hidden graph sizes and query counts, and cap memory at full-USA scale. gVisor wall-clock noise is unmeasured, so run the spike's 10% noise check under gVisor. It sits next to AlgoTune's Dijkstra task (0.201), but the deliverable differs. The reference is not written yet.
